newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba denies change in Spain's visa policy.
newsitem.headline: Cuba denies change in Spain's visa policy.

text.p: Cuba, in a diplomatic dispute with Spain, denied rumours on Wednesday that Spain had changed its visa policy, while Madrid accused Havana of manufacturing the dispute as a distraction from troubles at home.
Cuban authorities also posted a heavy security cordon around the Spanish Embassy building, closing off streets to traffic in the immediate area to prevent any disturbances.

Several hundred people gathered around the embassy on Tuesday following news that Cuba had protested strongly to the Spanish government over what it viewed as meddling in its internal affairs. Cuba said it was withdrawing its official approval for a new Spanish ambassador.

The Cuban Foreign Ministry issued a statement on Wednesday saying that in response to a request from the Spanish Embassy it was informing the public that the Spanish consular service was operating normally. Opening hours and procedures for visa requests and other embassy business were unchanged, it said.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs adds that rumours of the granting of visas by this (Spanish) consulate in a more rapid or special way are totally false," the statement added.
Relations between Spain and Cuba, which have strong historical, cultural and economic ties, are at their lowest point since 1990, when there was a crisis over asylum-seekers.

In Madrid, Spain accused Cuban leader Fidel Castro on Wednesday of manufacturing a diplomatic crisis with Madrid as a distraction from domestic troubles and said it did not rule out expelling the Cuban ambassador.

"All options are open," Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told a radio interviewer who asked him whether such an expulsion was possible. He later voiced concern to reporters that Cuba would sink into chaos if a transition to democracy on the Communist-ruled island was not completed before Castro goes.

"If this peaceful evolution is not achieved, when Castro disappears there will be upheavals, clashes, settling of scores and even spilling of blood, and that would not be a good scenario for Spanish business in Cuba," he said.

Tuesday's move by Cuba followed steady criticism of Castro's communist government by the conservative government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, which has adopted a tougher line on Havana than its Socialist predecessor.
